name: Anti-consumerism
summary: Anti-consumerism opposes a social and economic order in which people are encouraged to acquire goods beyond need or to display status. Its most developed themes are criticism of advertising, the ecological cost of overconsumption, voluntary simplicity, and doubts that growth or green technology alone can fix this. It is a cultural and ethical critique more than a full political programme, so it has little to say on many questions of state and regime.
scope: Modern anti-consumerism as a loose movement: Thoreau's Walden, Veblen's critique of conspicuous consumption, voluntary simplicity (Gregg, Elgin), Naomi Klein's No Logo, Stiegler, and the degrowth current. Excludes narrowly religious asceticism and primitivism; most answers on matters outside consumption and economy are inferred and low confidence.

keyFigures.name: Henry David Thoreau
keyFigures.role: Author of Walden, whose experiment in simple living is a founding text of the tradition.

keyFigures.name: Thorstein Veblen
keyFigures.role: Economist who analysed conspicuous consumption in The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899).

keyFigures.name: Naomi Klein
keyFigures.role: Author of No Logo (2000), a key anti-corporate, anti-brand work.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Adherents split: some want fair pay, others want less dependence on wage income and spending altogether, so the issue is not defining.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The movement blames profit-driven markets for manufacturing wants and ignoring public good, though some Austrian-leaning critics dissent.

public-ownership.rationale: Anti-consumerism targets consumption culture rather than ownership forms; adherents range from socialists to localists.

property-fundamental.rationale: Thoreau warns of possessions as fetters; adherents treat property as less sacred than a life of sufficiency, an inference.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Concern centres on firms pursuing profit at public expense, and adherents favour curbs such as limits on advertising.

worker-ownership.rationale: Some strands (commoning, cooperatives) favour it but it is not central to the consumption critique.

state-harmful.rationale: Anti-consumerism is not anti-state; many adherents want policy such as ad limits and degrowth measures, so they reject abolition.

traditional-family.rationale: Adherents include religious traditionalists and secular progressives; the movement itself is neutral.

more-religion-public.rationale: Religious figures like Francis and Gandhi inspire it, but secular strands are equally prominent.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The movement opposes cultural homogenisation by globalised brands, but it is not nationalist; adherents are split.

free-trade.rationale: The movement is tied to anti-globalisation and objects to globalised corporate trade and cultural homogenisation.

limit-growth.rationale: The degrowth and steady-state current in the scope holds that overconsumption drives ecological damage, but the only source is the degrowth article and branding-focused critics such as Klein do not target growth itself.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Overconsumption is seen as a root of climate change and adherents want consumption cut, not left to green tech alone.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Sources say green technology alone cannot solve consumption-driven problems; Thoreau warned men become tools of their tools.

revolution-justified.rationale: Mostly reformist and lifestyle-based; some radicals differ, so split.

central-planning.rationale: Degrowth stresses democratic decision-making rather than command planning, an inference for the wider movement.

socialized-markets.rationale: Adherents divide between market socialism, commoning and a general doubt of markets.

basic-income.rationale: Basic income is a common degrowth proposal; extending it to anti-consumerism as a whole is an inference.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Opposes globalised trade but protectionism is not an anti-consumerist programme.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Mainstream anti-consumerism wants reduced consumption, not abolition of money; only radical strands go further.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Austrian-leaning critics and others differ; no common line.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Foreign to the movement's grassroots outlook.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The critique concerns consumption, not forms of head of state, so adherents are indifferent.

democracy-best.rationale: Degrowth emphasises democratic decision-making, though the ideology as a whole says little about regime type.

direct-votes.rationale: Degrowth favours deliberative and participatory forums, an inference for the broader movement.

right-to-secede.rationale: Secession is unrelated to the critique of consumer culture; adherents are not united on it.

political-violence-never.rationale: Gandhian and religious roots (Gregg, Gandhi) lean nonviolent; some radicals dissent.

war-builds-character.rationale: Simple-living is associated with anti-war movements.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Some adherents are Marxists, but Marxists also criticise anti-consumerism; split.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Thoreau and the religious tradition treat acquisitive self-regard and wealth-chasing as the root of quiet desperation.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Linked to deep ecology and harmony with nature in simple-living thought.

limit-population.rationale: Rees and Hern write on limits to growth, but population control is contested among adherents.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Critics call it anti-modern, but mainstream adherents seek reform of consumer culture rather than call all industrial civilisation a disaster.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Sources say technology alone is insufficient and the movement opposes ever-faster consumption cycles.

restore-past-order.rationale: Not restorationist; reform-oriented, though religious strands sometimes appeal to tradition.

results-over-ideology.rationale: The movement is value-driven but has no stated stance on pragmatism versus ideology.

direct-action.rationale: Culture jamming, subvertising and boycotts are characteristic tactics.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Simple living means fewer possessions, not abandonment of agriculture or settled life; only fringe primitivists dissent.

production-for-use.rationale: Critique centres on profit-driven production creating artificial wants, favouring production for need.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Marxists see it as ignoring this; the movement targets profit over public good without a theory of exploitation.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: The sources link consumerism to waste and ecological harm, not to imperialism and great-power war.

taxation-theft.rationale: Tax-resistance is associated with some simple-living strands, but the mainstream wants public policy.

state-as-business.rationale: Opposes treating public life as commerce; critics of consumer culture reject citizens-as-customers framing.

media-academia-power.rationale: Not a stated view though media critique exists.

bound-labor.rationale: Opposed to coerced labour; Thoreau's emphasis on independence.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Postmodern strands accept it, but not a shared doctrine.

universal-morality.rationale: Religious strands say yes, postmodern strands say no; split.

single-common-good.rationale: The movement criticises profit over the public good but takes no position on unitary versus plural politics.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Diaspora citizenship rights are unrelated to the movement's concerns.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Degrowth calls for democratising economic relations.

school-vouchers.rationale: Education finance is not a theme; adherents differ on markets in schooling.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Austrian-leaning critics oppose stimulating consumption but others differ; split.

dominated-front.rationale: Anti-Western fronts are a different tradition; anti-consumerism has no stated view.

ban-interest.rationale: Some religious strands object to usury and debt, but not shared.

state-class-instrument.rationale: A Marxist theory of the state is not shared by the movement, and Marxists in fact criticise it.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Opposes overconsumption as a driver of climate change and resource depletion.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Distrust of corporate power is central, but elites in politics are not the focus.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Adherents want regulation of advertising and corporate conduct.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Debates about building socialism in one country belong to Marxism, not this movement.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Animal-rights ties exist but a legal ban is not doctrine.

population-transfer.rationale: Forced minority removal has no support in the movement's sources, but the movement does not engage with it either, so this is a low-confidence rejection from its nonviolent roots.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Status competition is the target in Veblen's account of emulation, and the movement criticises competitive acquisition.

party-controls-media.rationale: Opposed to controlled media; adherents criticise corporate control of media and advertising and would not substitute state control.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Naturalisation rules are unrelated to the consumption critique.

clerical-rule.rationale: Religious figures inspire it but it does not seek clerical rule.

people-in-arms.rationale: An armed citizenry is not an anti-consumerist idea.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Not a doctrine; Thoreau discusses owning housing but not banning rent.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Thoreau and simple-living tradition favour life close to nature, though not a modern doctrine.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Opposes homogenisation, but no stated view on ranking.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Commodification critiques cut both ways; split.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Citizenship law is unrelated to the consumption critique.

minority-language-support.rationale: Opposes cultural homogenisation by global brands, so supports linguistic diversity by inference.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Thoreau decries fashion-following and conformity; the movement values authentic living apart from consumer norms.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Poor-country debt relief is not specifically addressed, though anti-globalisation links might sympathise.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Growth is the target of the critique, so growth cannot justify restrictions.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Territorial claims in peace deals are unrelated to the movement.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Classification of the USSR is a Marxist debate outside this movement.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental concern and doubts that technology solves problems support acting before certainty.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Annexation law is unrelated to the movement's concerns.

character-from-environment.rationale: Sources say advertising and culture shape wants and the self, so character is formed by surroundings.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A Maoist theory not engaged by anti-consumerism.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Historical materialism is not an anti-consumerist tenet, and Marxists dispute the movement's emphasis on values and culture.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Simple living favours self-sufficiency at the household and local level, but not autarkic blocs with colonies.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Anti-globalisation and environmental strands favour binding standards on trade.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Opposed to violent minority action; Gandhian roots.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Some say consumerism can be separated from capitalism, others not; split.

delink-world-market.rationale: Degrowth strands are sympathetic, but the broader movement is not committed.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Anti-consumerism is commonly linked with animal rights.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Animal-rights links push against, but simple-living adherents farm; split.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Opposes display of wealth but not framed as an obligation; split.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Thoreau withdrew to Walden, yet the movement is also actively political; split.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Stiegler and others argue advertising and media damage development and sustain consumption.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Simple living values self-reliance, but not as national aid policy.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Domestic violence policy is unrelated to the consumption critique.

paid-care-work.rationale: Degrowth's four-in-one model values care work, but payment is not a common view.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Foreign ownership of strategic firms is not specifically addressed, though anti-globalisation sentiment might lean sympathetic.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Voluntary simplicity and the critique of conspicuous consumption (Veblen, Thoreau) hold that consumer culture is wasteful and harmful to people and society.

single-official-language.rationale: Anti-consumerism is a cultural critique of consumption with no language policy, and adherents are not united on it.

corporate-influence.rationale: Advertising and corporate marketing are the movement's main targets, so adherents see business power over public life as excessive.

industrial-unions.rationale: Union structure is not an anti-consumerist issue.

local-production.rationale: Degrowth and simple-living writers favour local production and short supply chains, a common anti-consumerist theme, but it is not central to the critique of consumption.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Anti-consumerism is a cultural critique and has nothing to say about deference between states; the issue is not defining.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: The movement has no position on regional revenue; degrowth stresses local self-reliance but not fiscal retention.

defeat-communism.rationale: Adherents split: the left of the movement is critical of capitalism but anti-consumerism has no stance on coexisting with communism.

religion-illusion.rationale: Religion is not a theme; Thoreau and simplicity traditions draw on spiritual ideas while many adherents are secular, so the movement is split.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: The movement criticises the consumer growth that capitalism produced and doubts that it builds a better society; some adherents grant its productive gains, so only mild disagreement.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Anti-consumerism does not address gender equality; adherents are split along general left and liberal lines.

socialized-care.rationale: No stated position; degrowth favours shared services and communal living but the movement as a whole does not address housework.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Not part of the consumption critique; split.

alienated-labor.rationale: Thoreau and Veblen describe work for status goods as alienating people from fuller living, in an older vocabulary.

social-market-economy.rationale: Degrowth critiques unlimited market growth but the sources set no model; split.

rich-first.rationale: Degrowth rejects growth-led policy as the route to well-being.

reification.rationale: Veblen and Stiegler describe how market society shapes desires and relations through things, though Marx's term is not the movement's own.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Adherents split: the movement is silent on policing, and anarchist strands favour abolition while most simplicity advocates do not discuss it.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: The movement has no position on constitutional design for divided societies; nothing in its sources addresses it.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Adherents split: ecological concern favours long-term risk reduction, but the movement focuses on overconsumption rather than extinction risk and often distrusts technology-led priorities.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Veblen's critique of the leisure class treats income from ownership without useful work as parasitic and wasteful.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Its central claim is that fulfilment lies beyond material acquisition, as in Thoreau and voluntary simplicity.

future-generations.rationale: The ecological cost of overconsumption is a developed theme, and degrowth stresses sustaining the planet for those to come.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Never addressed; the movement includes both statist and anarchist strands, so the answer is genuinely split.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Voluntary simplicity and Thoreau stress individuals and communities choosing their own way of living and producing, without a fixed blueprint.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Anti-consumerism and degrowth criticise reducing nature to market value and treating it as a growth resource.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Never addressed; adherents split on regional exploitation analysis, so left neutral.

farm-price-support.rationale: Not a theme; adherents favour local and small-scale farming but have no agreed view on price supports.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Degrowth and the critique of overconsumption put ecological limits above unlimited consumer freedom, though the movement stresses voluntary choice.

simple-living.rationale: Voluntary simplicity is central, urging fewer possessions, limited needs and self-sufficiency, as Thoreau advised in Walden.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Left-leaning adherents favour public provision of needs, others favour simple voluntary living; not a defining issue.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: The movement does not address religious politics; adherents are split.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Adherents split between technological optimists in degrowth and those favouring a simpler, low-tech life; no common line.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Veblen and Thoreau did not rest their critique on a labour theory of value; some strands do and others do not.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Anti-consumerism is not tied to patriotism either way; the movement is mostly indifferent to national feeling.

missingStatements.text: Advertising aimed at the public should be strictly limited by law.
missingStatements.rationale: Advertising is the most developed anti-consumerist theme, criticised for equating happiness with possessions and for intrusive public ads.

missingStatements.text: People should deliberately reduce what they own and buy, even if they could afford more.
missingStatements.rationale: Voluntary simplicity is central, urging fewer possessions and lower spending, as Thoreau advised.

missingStatements.text: Buying expensive goods mainly to display status is wasteful and harms society.
missingStatements.rationale: Veblen's conspicuous consumption and emulation argument holds such display is wasteful and drives status competition.

missingStatements.text: Working hours should be reduced so that people need and earn less.
missingStatements.rationale: Simple living and degrowth both link lower consumption to less paid work and more time for other pursuits.
missingStatements.declined: Hours reduction is a degrowth and labour-policy position more than a core anti-consumerist claim, and is not captured by a clean neutral statement without bloating the bank.

notes: Anti-consumerism is a cultural critique that can sit alongside socialist, Gandhian, religious, localist or even Austrian-economics views, so many non-economic answers are 0 or low confidence. Marxists and libertarians both criticise it.
